metadata.scenario_context: Carly, a single mom working two jobs, has been invited to an old friend's wedding

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Thailand strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Taiwan ROC strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Suggest giving money as a gift for Carly's friend's wedding,
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what should be the suitable gift for Carly's friend's wedding.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Alex, I heard Carly's going to her friend's wedding. You think it might be a good idea to give money as a gift? It could really help her out with expenses. 

Also, doesn’t it seem like when a mother works for pay, the children suffer? I just can’t shake that thought…
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Taiwan ROC.
shared_prefix.message:
Money as a gift can be practical, but maybe something more personal would be better. A thoughtful gift shows you care. How about a nice set of kitchenware or a gift card for a nice dinner? 

As for working mothers, that's just not true. A mother working can teach children about responsibility and independence. They can thrive with a working parent.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message: I see what you're saying, Alex. A personal gift can definitely show care. But I just feel like, deep down, we are all the same in wanting to support our friends in practical ways. And when it comes to working mothers, it’s interesting how we both have different views. At the end of the day, some values are just universal, like wanting the best for our children. I guess we all want them to thrive, no matter the situation, right?
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Taiwan ROC.
turns.message:
Supporting friends is important, but practical gifts don't always convey personal care. A heartfelt gift can mean more. 

About working mothers, I still believe that they can excel and raise well-adjusted children. It's not just about providing; it's about being present and involved, even through work. Many children benefit from seeing their mothers as strong role models.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
turns.message:
I understand the idea of heartfelt gifts, but giving money is just a straightforward way to help with a wedding, especially for someone like Carly who's juggling so much already. 

And about working mothers... I don't know. I still think that when they work for pay, it's hard for them to be fully present. It’s complicated. Children miss out on valuable time with their parents, don't you think?
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Taiwan ROC.
turns.message:
I get that giving money seems simple, but a thoughtful gift can still help Carly feel supported and appreciated. It’s about the meaning of the gesture, not just the practicality. 

Regarding working mothers, they can absolutely be present in meaningful ways, even while working. Kids can learn valuable lessons from a mother who balances work and family. It’s not always a negative impact; many children thrive in such environments.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
turns.message:
Sure, a thoughtful gift can have meaning, but sometimes practicality is what people really need. Money can relieve stress, especially for someone like Carly. 

As for working mothers, I just can’t help but feel that the absence can lead to struggles for children. I mean, it’s a balance, but the ideal scenario still seems to be having a mother at home when possible. Don’t you think the children lose something in that dynamic?
turns.label: Defense

About working mothers, I still believe children can gain a lot from having a working parent. They see dedication and hard work. It's not just about physical presence; it’s about quality time and the lessons learned. Children can thrive in diverse family dynamics, and many do.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.

turns.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Taiwan ROC.
turns.message:

Many children from working families grow up to be resilient and successful, showing that a working mother can be a strong influence.
